question: How many cups of tea do people in the United Kingdom drink per day?

target.what: Total number of cups of tea consumed by people in the United Kingdom (UK) on an average day, counting all tea types (black, green, herbal, fruit, decaffeinated) prepared as cups/mugs, including tea drunk at home and out of home, by residents and visitors present in the UK
target.publisher: No single official publisher; UK Tea & Infusions Association (UKTIA) is the commonly cited industry source, with ONS/Nielsen/Defra data as supporting inputs
target.cadence: Irregular industry estimates; consumption surveys annual; retail sales data monthly/quarterly
target.caveats: Ambiguity between cups and mugs, and between tea prepared from tea bags/loose leaf versus all hot infusions. Working interpretation: all cups/mugs of tea (including herbal/fruit) consumed per day, averaged over a year, UK-wide. Alternative narrower interpretation: black tea only, or tea bags only. A

candidates.hypothesis: UKTIA and predecessors have periodically published headline estimates of daily cups of tea drunk in the UK (e.g. ~100 million cups/day figures widely cited). These give a direct anchor for the target and its trend; the role is to provide a base level and recent direction.
candidates.data_to_find: Most recent UKTIA (or Tea Council) statement of daily cups of tea consumed in the UK, with date and definition (cups vs mugs, all tea vs black tea). Also any earlier published figures to establish trend. Substitute: press articles citing UKTIA figures with dates.

assessment.note: All four are the same ~100 million cups/day UK headline, ultimately traceable to UKTIA/ITC industry estimates. They are not independent measurements; they corroborate a stable industry anchor but share a single underlying source lineage.
Both give 36 billion cups/year, the annualised form of the ~100 million/day figure (36bn/365 ≈ 98.6m). Same ITC/UKTIA lineage, so redundant with p1/p22/p38/p102.
p28 is the arithmetic result of the Aldi methodology (31,758,667 adults × 55% × 4 cups). p24 is the rounded headline. They are the same calculation, not independent evidence.

Internally consistent Aldi survey chain: adult population × tea-preferring share × 4 cups/day. The 127m figure is a survey-based estimate that conflicts in level with the ~100m industry anchor, but uses a different method (self-reported cups among tea preferrers) and a different population base.

Industry anchor ~100m/day vs Aldi survey-derived 127m/day. The gap likely reflects methodology: Aldi applies 4 cups/day to 55% of adults (a high per-drinker rate and a broad prevalence), while the industry figure is a long-standing round number. Material disagreement to be resolved or bracketed.
Apparent consumption 113kt ≈ imports 133kt − exports 20kt = 113kt. Internally consistent physical-flow identity for 2015.
Per-capita 1,941 g/yr × ~65m population ≈ 126kt, roughly consistent with the 113kt apparent consumption (order-of-magnitude agreement, different years/sources).

Statista 72m kg/yr (excluding herbal/RTD/instant) is well below the 113kt apparent consumption; scope differences (exclusions, retail vs total) explain much of the gap. Use with caution as a lower-bound retail proxy.
YouGov age-cohort daily tea-drinking shares (11–32%) are mutually consistent and show a clear age gradient; they are one survey family, not independent of each other.

YouGov 2015 per-capita 884 cups/yr and age-band weekly rates are internally consistent (over-55s 21/wk, 18–24s 8/wk). Older vintage; useful for calibrating grams-per-cup and prevalence, not for direct current level.
p85 is the arithmetic conversion of p84 at 3g/teabag; same source (Kantar). Confirms a ~3g-per-cup conversion factor and a declining-volume trend signal.

Kantar 18.3bn tea occasions/yr and £663m spend are from the same Kantar dataset; occasions (~50m/day) are far below cups because occasions ≠ cups. Useful as a lower bound on drinking events, not cups.

36 billion cups/year is the annualised form of ~100m cups/day (36bn/365 ≈ 98.6m). Same ITC source; redundant with the daily headline.
2015 apparent consumption (113kt) is consistent with imports 133kt minus exports 20kt. Internally coherent physical-flow set for 2015, but old and pre-dating the target year.
Both give 72 million kg/year UK tea consumption (Statista, excluding herbal/RTD/instant). Same source, duplicate. Useful as a volume anchor for black/leaf tea only.

These are partner-level rows of the same 2023 HS090230 black-tea import table; they sum to the World total p112. Not independent; p112 is the usable aggregate. Note HS090230 covers only packaged black tea, understating total tea imports.
Same YouGov statistic (41% drink tea at home/work at least twice a day), duplicated. Measures a frequency threshold, not prevalence or cups/day.

YouGov 2015 survey: 884 cups/person/year overall, with 21 cups/week for over-55s and 8 for 18-24s. Internally consistent age gradient; old but a usable per-capita anchor needing trend adjustment.

Out-of-home tea share differs by metric: 4.1%/3.8% of servings (p78/p79) versus 17% of spend (p175). Different denominators (servings vs spend, and tea cheaper than coffee), so not a true contradiction but must not be mixed.

methods.label: m1
methods.rationale: Uses the most recent UKTIA/ITC headline (~100m cups/day) as the direct anchor. These are repeated versions of one industry estimate, so this is a single-source level, not an average of independent measurements; it may be stale and slightly high if consumption has continued to decline.
notes: p1: period 2023-08-22..2023-08-22 is not the same calendar period as 2026-01-01..2026-12-31
p22: period 2022-05-21..2022-05-21 is not the same calendar period as 2026-01-01..2026-12-31
p102: period 2024-05-01..2024-05-31 is not the same calendar period as 2026-01-01..2026-12-31

methods.label: m2
methods.rationale: High-end scenario from the Aldi 127m headline. Its methodology (4 cups/day for 55% of adults) is aggressive and excludes children, so it likely overstates; included as an upper-leaning independent survey-based route rather than a central estimate.

methods.label: m3

p45.role: UK annual tea consumption in kg (Statista, excl. herbal/RTD/instant)

a1.role: grams of dry tea per cup

methods.rationale: Volume route: convert annual kg of tea to cups via grams-per-cup, divide by days, and gross up for out-of-home tea not captured in retail volume. p45 excludes herbal/RTD/instant, so it understates all-tea scope; the out-of-home gross-up partly compensates. Main uncertainties are grams-per-cup and the out-of-home share.
methods.error: formula: numeric constant 1000 not allowed (only 1 and exponents); make it a named input. If the number only converts units (1000 g per kg, days per year), drop it and set the method's "unit" to the unit the formula then gives (e.g. 'g/day'); code converts it to 'cup/day'

methods.label: m4

p63.role: 2015 YouGov cups of tea per person per year

methods.rationale: Per-capita survey route: 884 cups/person/year (2015) adjusted downward for the observed long-run decline and scaled to current UK population. Depends on the trend factor and population assumptions; the 2015 base may already be dated.

inputs_detail.name: p63
inputs_detail.unit: cups of tea per person per year

methods.label: m5

a6.role: share of UK adults drinking tea daily

a5.role: mean cups/day among daily tea drinkers

methods.rationale: Base-rate route: population × daily-drinker prevalence × mean cups per daily drinker. Prevalence is anchored on YouGov age-band shares (p52/p54/p56/p58) and the cup rate on the 3+/5–10 cup distribution (p23/p161). Ignores occasional (non-daily) drinkers, so it may understate slightly; the 98% UKTIA prevalence (p104) is rejected as implausible.
methods.error: formula_mc must use at least one kept observed data point (a formula made only of assumptions is rejected)

kept.name: Grams of tea per cup (dry leaf, all tea types)
kept.rationale: p85 uses 3g per teabag as the industry convention; herbal/fruit and green teas use less leaf per cup and loose-leaf varies, so a central 2.5g with a wide range brackets the 3g teabag convention.
kept.applies_when: Converting dry tea mass to cups for all tea types averaged over the year.
kept.falsified_by: A current UK survey or industry statement giving grams per cup materially outside 1.8–3.5g.

kept.name: Out-of-home share of total UK tea cups
kept.rationale: p50/p147 show only 16% of tea drinkers buy tea out of home weekly, and p78/p79 show tea is a small share of out-of-home hot drinks; most tea is drunk at home. A modest out-of-home fraction is consistent with these.
kept.applies_when: Grossing at-home retail tea volume up to total consumption including foodservice.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that out-of-home tea is a much larger share of total cups (e.g. >30%).

kept.name: Trend factor: 2026 vs 2015 per-capita tea consumption
kept.rationale: UK tea consumption has been slowly declining (p84/p85 show a steep 2018 volume fall; coffee substitution noted in d6). Applying a modest decline factor to the 2015 YouGov per-capita figure (p63) brings it toward the target year.
kept.applies_when: Adjusting the 2015 per-capita cups figure to 2026.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that UK per-capita tea consumption has been flat or rising since 2015.

kept.name: UK population 2026
kept.rationale: No kept point gives current UK population; ONS mid-year estimates put the UK around 68–69 million in the mid-2020s. Used to scale per-capita cups to a national total.
kept.applies_when: Scaling a per-person cups figure to the whole UK population.
kept.falsified_by: An ONS population estimate for 2026 outside 67–71 million.

kept.name: Mean cups per day among daily tea drinkers
kept.rationale: p23/p160 show 35% of tea drinkers have 3+ cups/day and p161 shows 20% have 5–10; a mean around 2.5 cups/day among daily drinkers is consistent with that right-skewed distribution.
kept.applies_when: Combining a daily-drinker prevalence with a per-drinker cup rate.
kept.falsified_by: A representative survey giving a mean cups/day among daily drinkers outside 1.8–3.5.

kept.name: Share of UK adults who drink tea daily (age-weighted)
kept.rationale: YouGov age-band daily shares (p52/p54/p56/p58) range 11–32%; weighting by UK age structure gives roughly a quarter of adults drinking tea daily. The 98% UKTIA claim (p104) is implausible and not used.
kept.applies_when: Building a base-rate estimate of daily tea drinkers.
kept.falsified_by: A representative survey showing daily tea-drinking prevalence well outside 18–33% of adults.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
